think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A patient with established active pulmonary and nodal granulomatous disease developing subacute destructive osteolytic arthritis of the ankle creates strong anchoring bias toward musculoskeletal dissemination of her primary infection; paradoxically, lack of response to first-line antimycobacterial therapy indicates either drug-resistant mycobacterial osteomyelitis or an opportunistic co-infection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission triage evaluation ends after ankle MRI and baseline thoracic CT/inflammatory markers, immediately prior to ultrasound-guided needle puncture biopsy, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), and surgical debridement.
3. Differential Distinctions: Tuberculous arthritis/osteomyelitis typically responds over time to active antimycobacterial therapy and produces caseating acid-fast lesions; pyogenic bacterial septic arthritis produces rapid purulent destruction with positive bacterial cultures; opportunistic cryptococcal osteomyelitis in non-HIV hosts displays soap-bubble osteolysis and encapsulated budding yeast on special fungal stains (PAS/PAM/mucicarmine).
case_prompt:
A 67-year-old female (38.6 kg, 153 cm) presented with a one-month history of progressive swelling and pain in the right ankle, resulting in impaired weight-bearing and difficulty ambulating. Ten months prior, she had been evaluated for cervical lymphadenopathy, and five months prior, she was diagnosed with secondary cavitary pulmonary disease requiring bronchoscopic interventions and ongoing multi-drug antimycobacterial pharmacotherapy. When her right ankle pain and swelling initially developed, a local facility attributed the joint swelling to dissemination of her known chronic pulmonary and nodal disease and recommended continuing her existing medical regimen; however, her symptoms progressively worsened without clinical improvement.
At presentation, she reported no cough, sputum, fever, chills, night sweats, diarrhea, chest pain, dyspnea, rash, or neurological symptoms. She had no history of trauma to the ankle and no history of malignancy, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, cytotoxic therapy, or corticosteroid use.
On physical examination, vital signs were normal (body temperature 37.0°C, pulse rate 80 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 124/87 mmHg). The right lateral ankle exhibited increased surface temperature, noticeable swelling, marked tenderness, and a positive ankle varus trigger test, with palpable dorsalis pedis pulses and normal distal capillary refill. Pulmonary, cardiovascular, and abdominal examinations were normal.
Triage laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 11.9 x 10^9/L with 83.20% neutrophils, hemoglobin 94 g/L, platelet count 416 x 10^9/L, ESR 105 mm/h, and CRP 57.82 mg/L. Serum tumor markers were normal. Chest CT demonstrated multiple nodules and cavitary lesions in both lung fields. MRI of the right ankle joint demonstrated patchy osteolytic signal abnormalities centered at the distal fibula with subarticular destruction, uneven synovial thickening, joint space narrowing, and multiple surrounding soft-tissue abscesses.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Given known active cavitary pulmonary and nodal disease, ankle swelling was initially presumed to be tuberculous dissemination; however, the lesion worsened despite ongoing multi-agent antimycobacterial therapy, and acid-fast stains and PCR of sputum and joint fluid were repeatedly negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: When her right ankle developed swelling and pain, she initially sought evaluation at a local hospital, where it was considered to be caused by tuberculosis. She was recommended to continue anti-tuberculosis treatment. However, with no significant clinical improvement, she sought further treatment at our hospital.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Subacute joint swelling with neutrophilic leukocytosis, marked ESR/CRP elevation, and periarticular abscesses on MRI suggested a secondary bacterial pyogenic process; however, multiple blood, sputum, and preliminary microbial cultures were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Several etiological examinations were conducted including blood culture, sputum culture, pneumococcal antigen test, legionella antigen test, fungi, parasites, mycoplasma test, Chlamydia antigen test, HIV antibodies test, Treponema pallidum test, serum hepatitis A, B, C, E tests, nucleic acid testing for COVID-19, Brucella IgG antibody test, acid-fast stain, and polymerase chain reaction for tuberculosis in sputum, but all results were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing of ankle puncture tissue identified Cryptococcus neoformans, confirmed by positive cryptococcal antigen testing and histopathology displaying micro-refractive spheres on PAS/PAM staining, establishing cryptococcal osteomyelitis co-occurring with chronic tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Ultimately, the non-HIV patient without underlying diseases was definitively diagnosed with Cryptococcal neoformans ankle osteomyelitis, concomitant with tuberculous lymphadenitis and secondary tuberculosis.

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case. Target canonical disease is Tuberculosis (with Cryptococcus neoformans osteomyelitis subtype). Prompt halts before mNGS, joint puncture biopsy, and fungal staining. Direct verbatim quotes provided.
